question: Depreciation appears on which financial statement(s)?
before: D&A is the ultimate linking item. P&L expense (reduces profit), BS accumulated depreciation (reduces net PP&E), CFS add-back (non-cash). Understanding this triple role is key to linking.
after:
Concept: Depreciation is a non-cash accounting allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life. Because it reduces reported profit but involves no actual cash outflow, it appears in different forms across all three financial statements, serving as a critical linking mechanism.

Step-by-step linkage:

1. Income Statement: Depreciation is recorded as an operating expense, reducing EBIT and net profit. This is the P&L charge.

2. Balance Sheet: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account that reduces the gross value of Property, Plant & Equipment to arrive at net PP&E (book value). This shows the cumulative wear over time.

3. Cash Flow Statement: Under the indirect method, depreciation is added back to net profit in the Operating Activities section because it was deducted as an expense but represents no actual cash outlay.

Why this is correct: Depreciation's role across all three statements is what ties them together. The P&L expense reduces profit; the BS accumulation shows the asset's declining book value; the CFS add-back reconciles accrual profit to actual cash generation. This triple appearance is fundamental to understanding how the statements link.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Only Income Statement — Ignores that depreciation also reduces asset values on the balance sheet and must be adjusted in the cash flow statement.

B) Only Balance Sheet — Misses that depreciation is a P&L expense and a critical cash flow adjustment; treating it as balance-sheet-only misunderstands its role in profit calculation.

D) Only Cash Flow Statement — Overlooks that depreciation is first recognized as an expense on the income statement and accumulated on the balance sheet before being reversed in cash flows.

Intuition: Depreciation is the bridge between accrual accounting (P&L and BS) and cash accounting (CFS). In equity research, recognizing where a non-cash charge appears helps you quickly spot how much profit is inflated and how much cash is actually being generated—the core of quality-of-earnings analysis.
